extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, students and readers of literary criticism and classical literature
extracted.subtask_description: An essayistic literary-criticism subtask: evaluating the moral, intellectual, and stylistic qualities of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations (and linked reflections on literary origins). The page provides standards for judging inward life, moral sincerity, emotional tone, and stylistic power in classical and English poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relatability to contemporary readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Marcus Aurelius 'becomes for us a man like ourselves, a man in all things tempted as we are' — the degree to which a historical figure's moral/intellectual life can be felt as close and relevant to modern readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare moral and intellectual proximity across figures (e.g., Marcus Aurelius vs. Saint Louis or Alfred); prefer subjects whose inward life presents universal temptations and concerns that modern readers can recognize and sympathize with.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the inward life (Meditations) as the best record
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The record of him on which his fame chiefly rests is the record of his inward life,--his Journal...’ — evaluate a man's greatness primarily by his private memoranda and inner reflections rather than outward incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give special weight to candid personal writings (journals, meditations) because they reveal character and provide 'priceless treasure' for those seeking right thinking and well-doing; outward exploits are secondary unless they illuminate inner life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and sincerity of personal writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Entries 'jotted down from day to day... meant for no eye but his own, without the slightest attempt at style' — value unadorned, sincere, and unselfconscious personal prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor writings that lack artifice and rhetorical striving; the absence of concern for polish can indicate authenticity and allow emotional/ethical force to come through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, purpose-driven moral economy
rubrics_metrics.description: The maxim 'Let nothing be done without a purpose' and the injunction to ask 'Is this one of the unnecessary things?' — judge moral writing and action by usefulness and avoidance of superfluity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether thoughts and acts are purposeful; prefer texts that actively eliminate unnecessary acts and unnecessary thoughts, thereby increasing leisure and reducing uneasiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selfless motive and intrinsic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal of acting like 'a vine which has produced grapes, and seeks for nothing more' — virtue enacted without desire for external reward or recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for evidence that good acts are done for their own sake rather than for recompense; texts or characters exhibiting this are judged more morally admirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional accent suffusing moral teaching
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘It is by its accent of emotion that the morality of Marcus Aurelius acquires a special character’ — the presence of a felt emotional tone that suffuses and dignifies moral precepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between intellectually persuasive moral writing and writing that moves the soul; prefer works whose emotional tone (tenderness, sweetness) deepens their ethical force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweetness combined with dignity
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'just admixture in the moral character of sweetness and dignity' — moral voice should blend gentleness with majesty or seriousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tonal balance: sweetness without loss of dignity is a marked merit; it allows tenderness to ennoble austerity rather than to subdue it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete list of practical virtues to exhibit
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit catalogue of virtues one should show: 'sincerity, gravity, endurance of labor, aversion to pleasure, contentment with thy portion and with few things, benevolence, frankness, no love of superfluity, freedom from trifling, magnanimity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this roster as a checklist of moral qualities to praise or expect in exemplary character or moral writing; lack of these traits marks voluntary moral failing rather than natural incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical and political contextualization of moral actions
rubrics_metrics.description: When judging actions such as the punishment of Christians, the essay insists on understanding the historical, political, and cultural context (e.g., Christians seen as politically subversive or secret societies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid presentism: interpret disputed historical actions by considering contemporaneous beliefs, political necessities, and common prejudices; do not automatically ascribe modern motives or moral categories to past actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of contemporaneous testimony as corroboration
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'clear consenting voice of all his contemporaries' is an important element in assessing a man's outward life and moral reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weight external, contemporary praise or criticism when reconstructing reputation — broad, cross-section testimony (high and low, friend and enemy) strengthens claims about character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transforming adversity into exercise for reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The Stoic idea: 'The ruling part of man can make a material for itself out of that which opposes it' — adversity and opposition should be employed as fuel for moral and rational growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge character and doctrine by their capacity to appropriate difficulties as practice for the reason; a worthy moral teaching makes hardships instruments of self-improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner retreat and concise foundational principles
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Nowhere either with more quiet or more freedom from trouble does a man retire than into his own soul... let thy principles be brief and fundamental' — value inward resources and compact guiding maxims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a thinker provides brief, fundamental principles that can be readily recalled and used to re-center the soul; inner retreat (mental solitude) is presented as available to all and a sign of maturity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility about fame and awareness of transience
rubrics_metrics.description: Passages emphasizing that worldly honors are 'empty, and rotten, and trifling' and that reputation is fleeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value moral perspectives that cultivate detachment from fame and possessions, and that rightly measure life's vanities to foster right living.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuous self-monitoring and self-questioning
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of asking 'About what am I now employing my soul?... whose soul have I now?' — ongoing inspection of one's ruling principle and state of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate moral seriousness by the presence of regular, rigorous self-examination aimed at correcting deviations of character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiated literary effects: intellect, character, soul
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparative claim: Seneca's sentences 'are stimulating to the intellect'; Epictetus 'fortifying to the character'; Marcus Aurelius 'find their way to the soul.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing philosophical or moral prose, classify its chief effect — intellectual stimulation, character-building force, or soulful emotional appeal — and judge success according to the intended effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of anachronistic moral condemnation
rubrics_metrics.description: The essay argues that modern readers commonly misjudge Marcus Aurelius' sanctioning of punishment because they imagine him 'fresh from the perusal of the Gospel' — a warning against retrojecting later moral knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should avoid attributing later theological or ethical knowledge to earlier figures; instead, evaluate according to the conceptual world available to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three formative English-poetry traits (style, melancholy, natural magic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim: English poetry derived 'its turn for style, its turn for melancholy, and its turn for natural magic' (the vivid rendering of nature) in large part from Celtic sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these three dimensions as distinct axes when tracing influences on English poetry: stylistic finesse, melancholic temperament, and a capacity for 'natural magic' or vivid nature-imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of style as the distinguishing poetic power
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'peculiar effect' produced by masters of style (Pindar, Virgil, Dante, Milton) is a distinct literary power; German poetry is said to be deficient in this highest sense of style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between clear/simple/passionate expression and the rarer 'eminent power of style' — when evaluating poetry, ask whether it attains that elevated, characteristic stylistic effect exemplified by the listed masters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for popular misrepresentation and novelty-based prejudice
rubrics_metrics.description: Explains why Christians were misrepresented (confusion with Jews, secretive assemblies, simplicity of theism) and how novelty provokes instinctive repugnance; this affects moral and historical evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging groups or doctrines, examine external causes of misrepresentation (confusion with other groups, secrecy, novelty) and temper moral judgment by awareness of social prejudice and fear of dissolution.
